questions.question: Why do we measure algorithm cost with Big O rather than timing the code with a clock?
options: Big O describes how work grows with input size, independent of the machine, language, or load, which wall-clock time cannot.
Big O gives the exact number of seconds a function takes.
Big O only applies to sorting algorithms.
questions.explanation: Wall-clock time depends on the hardware, the language, and the current load, so it is not portable or stable. Big O captures the growth rate of the operation count as input size grows, which is a property of the algorithm itself.
questions.misconception: Big O is not a running time in seconds. It is a growth rate that ignores constants and hardware.

questions.question: A function has one loop over n items and, inside it, another loop over the same n items. What is its time complexity?
questions.explanation: Nested loops multiply: for each of n outer steps you do n inner steps, so the total is n times n, which is O(n squared). Big O drops constant factors, so O(2n) would simplify to O(n) and is not how nesting works.

questions.scenario: You must check membership (is x present?) millions of times against a large collection that does not change.
questions.question: Which structure gives the best average lookup, and why?
options: A list, because lists are faster for everything.
A set or dict, because hash lookup is average O(1), versus O(n) for scanning a list.
A tuple, because tuples are immutable and therefore faster to search.
It does not matter, since all lookups are O(1).
questions.explanation: A set or dict uses hashing, so an average membership test is O(1) regardless of size. Scanning a list or tuple is O(n) because it checks elements one by one. For heavy repeated membership tests, the set wins decisively at scale.
questions.misconception: Immutability (tuple) does not make membership faster. The data structure's lookup mechanism (hashing versus linear scan) is what matters.

questions.question: Explain the difference between best, average, and worst case complexity, and say which one Big O usually reports and why.
questions.answer: Best case is the fewest operations for a lucky input, worst case is the most for the hardest input, and average case is the expected cost over typical inputs. Big O usually reports the worst case, because it gives a guarantee that the algorithm never does more than that, which is what you need to reason about reliability at scale.
questions.explanation: Average case matters in practice too (for example, hash lookups are average O(1) but worst-case O(n) under collisions), so state which case you mean when it differs.
